en: A Commentary on the Mahāyāna Śālistamba Sūtra Following Its Study:
A Prostration with Reverence to the Samyaksaṃbuddha and the Assembly of the Sublime Dharma and Saṅgha.
Regarding all the unresolved meanings within the *Śālistamba*, I shall now provide a brief explanation in successive order.
Among the sixteen philosophical systems, the first is the theory that the effect exists within the cause (*satkāryavāda*).
This refers to certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who give rise to such a view and establish this doctrine.
At all times and at every moment,
the nature of the effect is fully present within all causes;
this is the view held by the Vārṣagaṇya heretics.
For what cause and condition do they give rise to such a conception and establish such a doctrine?
This demonstrates that the effect exists within the cause,
both by means of scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
As for scripture, it refers to the scriptural collections (*śāsana-piṭaka*) composed by those former masters.
This was transmitted through successive lineages down to the present day,
demonstrating that the nature of the fruit exists prior within the cause.
"Principle" (nyāya) refers to the nature of those very śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who abide in investigation and analysis;
that is, they abide in the stage of reflection (vitarka-bhūmi), abide in the stage of self-discernment (sva-vibhaṅga-bhūmi), and abide in the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana-bhūmi).
Following his contemplative observation of the stages of practice, he reflects thus:
"If this dwelling arises from that nature."
It is universally known and established by all the world that this is the cause for that effect and no other;
furthermore, those who seek a result rely solely on this cause and no other.
Furthermore, it is precisely through the application of effort and construction toward those [causes] that the sought-after effects are achieved, and not otherwise.
Moreover, if those effects arise from those very causes and do not arise from anything else,
then those effects must already exist within the cause.
If it were not so, one would have to establish that everything is the cause of everything;
for the sake of seeking a single result, everything would have to be applied toward everything.
When effort is applied to construction,
it should arise from every [cause] as every fruit;
thus it is by way of designation.
Because it seeks its object;
because its activity is determined;
and because it arises.
Since he perceives that the nature of the effect is always present within the cause,
one should question him as follows:
"What is your position?"
What is the characteristic of the cause?
What is the characteristic of the fruit?
Are these two characteristics of cause and fruit different or not different?
If there were no distinct characteristics,
then the two categories of cause and effect would not exist;
for it is because cause and effect are definitively without distinction that these two categories [would otherwise be established].
It is not logical for the effect to exist within the cause.
If there were a difference in their characteristics,
what would you think?
Regarding the characteristic of the effect within the cause,
is it an unarisen characteristic or an already-arisen characteristic?
If it is an unarisen characteristic...
It would be unreasonable to say that the effect exists within the cause while it has not yet arisen;
for if the characteristic of having already arisen were itself the effect, [it could not exist within the cause].
It is not logical that what has already arisen should arise again from a cause; therefore,
the effect does not pre-exist within the cause.
However, there must be causes and conditions for an effect to arise;
furthermore, there are phenomena characterized by marks,
and within these phenomena characterized by marks...
It can be understood through five aspects that it is obtainable in a single location.
Like water in a bottle,
it is obtainable in its support;
like visual consciousness in the eye.
Third, it is obtainable through its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
such as [knowing] a cause by its own nature without relying on inference.
Fourth, it is obtainable through its own activity (*svakarma*).
Fifth, because of the transformation of the cause, there is transformation;
or, because of the transformation of conditions, the effect undergoes transformation.
Therefore, they assert that the effect exists within the cause at all times and for all eternity.
This is not reasonable; for this reason,
the argument you have established is not stated in accordance with logic.
Thus, because it is not of a different characteristic,
because it is of a different characteristic,
and because it is of an unarisen characteristic.
Because it would possess the characteristic of having already arisen,
this is not logical. The proponent states that the two terms are manifested through conditions.
It is just as there might be a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena exists;
it is manifested through various conditions,
but is not produced by those conditions.
That is to say, those who maintain the theory that the effect exists within the cause,
as well as those who maintain the theory of the characteristics of sound, hold such a view.
For what reason and by what causal conditions does the proponent maintain that the effect exists within the cause?
Do you see that within all causes there first exists the nature of the fruit,
which is then manifested by conditions?
This is due to both scripture and reasoning.
Scripture is as previously explained.
As for reasoning, it refers to the case where there is a certain individual whose nature is such that...
Its nature is reflection and investigation, as explained in detail previously.
He reflects in this way:
"The fruit existed prior [to its production]."
Furthermore, it would be illogical for it to arise again from causes; yet,
it is not the case that effort is unnecessary for the accomplishment of the result.
For what reason, moreover, would they exert effort?
Is it not solely for the sake of manifesting the fruit? Having made such false conceptualizations, they establish the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti-vāda*).
One should question him thoroughly:
"What do you intend? Is it by way of an unobstructing condition that it acts as an obstruction, or by way of an obstructing condition?
If it is by way of an unobstructing condition, [then...]
It is not logical for that which is a non-obstructing condition to act as an obstruction.
If there were obstructing conditions, [it would be logical].
Why does a cause that belongs to its own fruit not act as an obstacle?
Because both are equally existent.
This is not logical.
For example, just as darkness obstructs the water within a basin,
it can also obstruct the basin itself.
If it is argued that the causes and conditions of an obstruction can also act as obstructions,
then those causes should also be made manifest.
Since both are equally obscured,
it is unreasonable to claim that [the statement] merely reveals that light exists within the cause and that the effect arises therefrom,
while failing to reveal the cause itself.
Furthermore, one should ask him:
"Is this nature itself the condition for obstruction, or is it something else?
If it is the case that this nature itself is the condition for obstruction, [then...]
In that case, existence itself would never be manifest,
which is unreasonable;
for the cause is also existent.
Why would it not constitute an obstruction?
If you say that the nature of the fruit is the condition for the obstruction, [then...]
Thus, a single dharma is both cause and effect;
for example, the sprout is the fruit of the seed,
and the stem and so forth are the fruits of the sprout.
Consequently, it would follow that a single phenomenon is both manifest and unmanifest,
which is unreasonable.
Furthermore, I now ask you:
Answer as you see fit:
Is the fundamental dharma (mūladharma) different from its manifestation (vyakti), or not?
If they are not different, [then...]
If phenomena were to manifest eternally,
such that what has already manifested manifests again,
it would not accord with reason.
If you say they are different,
is that [difference] manifested as being without cause,
or is it with cause?
If one says it is without cause,
that it manifests without a cause, this is not logical.
If there were a cause, the nature of the effect could be manifested; it is not,
however, the nature of the cause.
It is not logical that what is unmanifest could manifest the effect;
thus, there is no obstructing condition.
Because there are obstructing conditions;
because there are characteristics; and because there are the characteristics of the fruit.
It is illogical [to claim] that they manifest as non-different or that they manifest as different.
Third, those who maintain the theory that the past and future truly exist:
That is to say, there may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who,
while abiding within this Dharma,
due to improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra), [fall into error].
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
that the past exists and the future exists, their characteristics being fully established,
just like the present, which is substantially real and not merely nominal.
For what reason does one give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine?
It is by means of both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
As for scripture, it is as previously explained.
Furthermore, those who abide in this dharma engage in improper conceptualization regarding the sūtras of the Tathāgata.
That is to say, as the Sūtra states:
"All that exists consists of the twelve bases (āyatana)."
The real nature of these twenty locations exists.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"Past karma exists."
Furthermore, it is said:
there is past form;
there is future form.
The detailed explanation extends even to consciousness, which is likewise.
As for the principle, it refers to one who is by nature prone to discursive thought and by nature prone to investigation,
as explained at length previously.
He thinks thus:
"If a phenomenon abides by its own characteristic,
that phenomenon truly exists."
If this were non-existent in the future,
then at that time it would not yet have received its characteristics;
if this were non-existent in the past, [then...]
At that time, it would lose its own characteristic.
If this were so, then the self-characteristic of each phenomenon (dharma) would not be established.
Because this principle is likewise not real,
it is not tenable; such is the reflection.
They give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
that the nature and characteristics of the past and future exist substantially.
One should question him carefully:
"What is your position regarding the two characteristics of the past and the future?"
Are the characteristics [of the past and future] identical to or different from the characteristic of the present?
If one says they are identical, then the characteristics of the three time periods would be established as one.
This is not logical.
If the characteristic were different [from the nature], then both the nature and the characteristic would be substantially existent.
This is not logical.
Furthermore, you should state what you yourself intend.
Following the dharmas of the three periods of time,
are they permanent or are they impermanent?
If it were of a permanent nature,
it would fall within the three periods of time,
which is not logical.
If the characteristic of impermanence were eternally and truly existent throughout the three periods of time.
This is not logical.
Furthermore, I now ask you;
answer as you see fit.
Is it that future dharmas are reckoned as having reached the present world?
Or is it that after dying there, they are born here?
Or do they simply abide in the future?
Is it that [the action] arises in the present by way of conditions?
Or is it that there was originally no action,
and now there is action?
Is it that the original characteristics were incomplete,
whereas now they are complete?
Or is it that the original characteristics are different?
Is this not, then, a different characteristic?
Does the present part exist within the future?
If it is the very same future dharma that comes and arrives in the present, [how can there be a distinction?]
This would then possess a specific location;
subsequently, it would be no different from the present,
and it would further follow that it is eternal.
This is not logical.
If one says that after death in the future, one is born in the present,
then it follows that there is no birth in the future.
In the present world, phenomena are fundamentally non-existent at birth;
furthermore, it is illogical to speak of death and passing away for that which has not yet arisen in the future.
